match.reason: The bank card teaches what makes a protected area work (size, connection and management) rather than the brief's point that protection works by limiting what people can do there, and it is written for Year 12 NSW rather than Year 10 Australian Curriculum.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question b, other: The clue ('the country holds the duty') all but states the right option, so a student can pick it without understanding World Heritage listing.
- Card, fact: 'Governments protect it' overgeneralises for Australia. Many protected areas in the National Reserve System are Indigenous Protected Areas dedicated by Traditional Owners, or private reserves, not only government-declared areas. Wording such as 'Governments or other groups, such as Traditional Owners' would be accurate.

rejected.title: Protected areas
card: A protected area is land or sea set aside to look after its environment. Governments protect it by limiting what people can do there.
National park
a land area where activities such as clearing, mining and hunting are restricted, while visitors can usually walk, camp and look at nature.
Marine reserve
an area of sea where activities such as fishing, drilling or anchoring may be limited to protect reefs and sea life.
World Heritage listing
a place recognised by UNESCO, a United Nations agency, as having global value for nature or culture. The country that holds it must work to protect it.
rejected.remember: Protected areas look after places by limiting what people can do in them.

a.q: Which of these is an example of how a marine reserve protects the environment?
opts: Fishing is limited in parts of it to protect reefs
Bush clearing and hunting on nearby land are restricted
The United Nations takes over running the area
All people are banned from ever entering the area
a.why: A marine reserve is an area of sea where some activities, such as fishing, are limited to protect sea life. Restricting clearing and hunting on land describes a national park, not a marine reserve. Protected areas limit what people do rather than shutting everyone out.
a.clue: Think about where a marine reserve is and how protection works.

b.q: A coastal reef is added to the World Heritage list because of its global value. What does this listing mean for the country that holds the reef?
opts: It must work to protect the reef for the future
It hands control of the reef to the United Nations
It must ban every visitor from the reef area
It is no longer allowed to make rules about the reef
b.why: World Heritage listing recognises global value and puts a duty on the country to protect the place. The country still manages it, and visitors may still be allowed with limits. The United Nations does not take control.
b.clue: The listing recognises value, and the country holds the duty.

a.q: Why does a government set up a marine reserve?
opts: To limit activities that could harm sea life and reefs
To give fishing boats free access to every part of the sea
To move the sea life to a safer area on land
To make the sea a place that only scientists may enter
a.why: A marine reserve protects ocean environments by limiting some activities, such as fishing or drilling. It does not remove all human use of the area, and it does not move wildlife elsewhere.
a.clue: Protection works by limiting what people can do.

b.clue: The listing recognises value, and the country holds the duty.

version.title: Protected areas
card: A protected area is land or sea set aside to look after its environment. Governments, or other groups such as Traditional Owners, protect it by limiting what people can do there.
National park
an area, mostly on land, where activities such as clearing, mining and hunting are restricted, while visitors can usually walk, camp and look at nature.
Marine reserve
an area of sea where activities such as fishing, drilling or anchoring may be limited to protect reefs and sea life.
World Heritage listing
a place recognised by UNESCO, a United Nations agency, as having global value for nature or culture. The country that holds it agrees to work to protect it.
version.remember: Protected areas look after places by limiting what people can do in them.

a.q: How does a marine reserve usually protect the environment?
opts: By limiting fishing in parts of it to guard reefs
By restricting bush clearing and hunting on land
By handing the area over to the United Nations
By banning all people from ever entering the area
a.why: A marine reserve is an area of sea where some activities, such as fishing, are limited to protect sea life. Restricting clearing and hunting on land describes a national park, not a marine reserve. Protected areas limit what people do rather than shutting everyone out.
a.clue: Where is a marine reserve, and what is limited there?

b.q: A coral reef off a country's coast is added to the World Heritage list for its global value. What does the listing mean for that country?
opts: It agrees to work to protect the reef for the future
It hands control of the reef to the United Nations
It has to ban every visitor from the reef area
It is no longer allowed to make rules about the reef
b.why: World Heritage listing recognises global value, and the country that holds the place agrees to work to protect it. The country still manages the reef, and visitors may still come with limits. The United Nations does not take control.
b.clue: Recall what UNESCO's listing asks of a place's own country.

a.best: By limiting fishing in parts of it to guard reefs

b.best: It agrees to work to protect the reef for the future
